requirement_title: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2283: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2283
Type: bug

## Requirement

Both `MessagePackGenerator` (CS8785) and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` (AD0001) throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` when a `[MessagePackObject]` type has a member whose type is a closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly.

Because the generator then "will not contribute to the output", the compiling assembly silently ends up with no generated resolver at all. It is only a warning, so a normal build looks fine, but trimmed and NativeAOT apps fail at runtime.

Repro: two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key);
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`.

Expected: a clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.

Actual:

```
CSC : warning CS8785: Generator 'MessagePackGenerator' failed to generate source. It will not
contribute to the output and compilation errors may occur as a result. Exception was of type
'IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the bounds of the array.'.
CSC : warning AD0001: Analyzer 'MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Analyzers.MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer'
threw an exception of type 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the
bounds of the array.'.
```

`app.dll` contains no `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`. Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8.

What triggers it (`Item` declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`):

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` | crash |
| `struct Item<T>` | crash |
| `struct Item` | ok |
| `record struct Item` | ok |
| `class Item<T>` | ok |
| `record class Item<T>` | ok |

It needs all three of: generic, value type, from a referenced assembly. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` makes the crash disappear.

Reporter's analysis: `CollectGeneric` line 661 is the closed-generic branch that calls `GetObjectInfo` directly, so `GetObjectInfo` runs against a type that has no syntax. Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()` like the neighbouring `GetIdentifierLocation` / `GetLocation` / `GetParameterListLocation` helpers. That collection is empty for a metadata symbol. The reporter did not narrow down which of the three fires.

Workaround: `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type short-circuits `CollectCore` before `GetObjectInfo` is reached.

## Acceptance criteria

- Building `app` from the repro produces no CS8785 warning. (derived)
- Building `app` from the repro produces no AD0001 warning from `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer`. (derived)
- `app.dll` contains a `GeneratedMessagePackResolver` (a generated resolver exists). (derived)
- The generator and analyzer do not throw on a closed generic struct or record struct declared in a referenced assembly.
- Closed generic classes, non-generic structs and types declared in the same assembly keep working as before (the "ok" rows in the table). (derived)
- Diagnostics that need a source location do not crash when the offending symbol has no declaring syntax (metadata symbol). (derived)

## Notes from discussion

No comments on the issue. The reporter points at `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` being indexed unguarded at TypeCollector.cs lines 735, 1009 and 1101, and notes the neighbouring helpers use `FirstOrDefault()`. Possibly related: #2092 (CS8785 from the v3 generator, different inner exception, no repro).

the change's own tests do not catch mutants at src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:239, 985, 1448; the existing suite does

receipt_plan.detail: TypeCollector.cs:239 negate-condition: this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, diagnostic); -> this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is not null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, diagnostic);; TypeCollector.cs:239 delete-statement: this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, diagnostic); -> (statement deleted); TypeCollector.cs:985 delete-statement: this.reportDiagnostic?.Invoke(Diagnostic.Create(MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull, GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item), formattedType.ToDisplayString(SymbolDisplayFormat.FullyQualifiedFormat), item.Name)); -> (statement deleted); TypeCollector.cs:1448 delete-statement: report(diagnostic); -> (statement deleted)

hunches.claim: The change also suppresses an error diagnostic for types declared in the compilation itself. `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` returns null when the property's declaring syntax is not a `PropertyDeclarationSyntax`. A positional record parameter declared with `[property: Key((string)null)]` is such a case: its syntax is a ParameterSyntax. The resulting null-location `BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull` diagnostic is then dropped by `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`, because `Location.None.IsInSource` is false. So the error is silently lost for a type declared in this project. That contradicts the requirement that same-assembly types keep their diagnostics and that only metadata symbols lose them.

receipt_plan.detail: VerifyCS test with LanguageVersion=Latest and SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck, using source `[MessagePackObject] public record R([property: Key((string)null)] string A);`. It expects the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull diagnostic. On head the diagnostic is absent (the test fails because an expected diagnostic is missing); on base the analyzer threw InvalidCastException.

hunches.claim: The new GetPropertyIdentifierLocation helper only handles PropertyDeclarationSyntax. A positional record property such as `record Cmd([property: Key((string)null)] string Scope)` is declared by a ParameterSyntax, so the helper returns null and the diagnostic gets Location.None. ReportIfLocatedInCompilation then drops it because Location.None is not IsInSource. BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull is therefore silently lost for a type declared in source in the compilation being analyzed. On base this case threw InvalidCastException; it should now be reported (for example at the parameter location), not suppressed.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.PositionalRecordNullKeyDiagnosticTests.NullStringKeyOnPositionalRecordPropertyIsReported. It runs MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer on a C# 9 positional record with [property: Key((string)null)] and asserts that a MsgPack diagnostic is reported in source on the `Scope` parameter. On head nothing is reported, so the test fails.

hunches.claim: The wrapper installed in the constructor drops every diagnostic whose location is not in a source tree of this compilation. That includes diagnostics about a [MessagePackObject] type that is declared in source, when the offending member has no syntax: for example a public, Key-less property inherited from a base class in a referenced assembly (MemberNeedsKey now gets a null location from FirstOrDefault). L8 only exempts types that are themselves metadata. Here the formatted type belongs to this compilation, so its MsgPack004 problem is now silently swallowed instead of being reported at the type's identifier.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile `public class Base { public int X { get; set; } }` into a MetadataReference. Analyze `[MessagePackObject] public class Derived : Base { [Key(0)] public int Y { get; set; } }` with MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer. Expect a MsgPack004 diagnostic in source (for example on `Derived`). On head expect none, if the collector enumerates inherited members.

hunches.claim: The new reportDiagnostic wrapper drops every diagnostic whose location is not in source within this compilation. Diagnostics created with a null or Location.None location (for example GetIdentifierLocation returning null for metadata types, or other paths with no location) used to be reported and are now silently suppressed. This is a behavior change for same-assembly types too. Previously reported location-less diagnostics, such as MsgPack003/004/005 errors, may no longer appear in users' builds, so invalid code could compile cleanly.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the analyzer tests for MsgPack003/004/005 and any diagnostic created with a null location (e.g. Diagnostic.Create with a null location from GetIdentifierLocation/GetLocation on a type in the same compilation). Assert the diagnostic is still reported on head as on base. Fail if any diagnostic with Location.None that base reported is now missing.

hunches.claim: The new ReportIfLocatedInCompilation wrapper drops every diagnostic whose Location is not in a syntax tree of the compilation, including Location.None. MsgPack00x diagnostics produced via GetLocation helpers that return null (metadata symbols) are silently suppressed. This is the intended fix and matches ledger L8, but the wrapper also suppresses any diagnostic with a null/None location for source types, such as when FirstOrDefault returns null. Diagnostics that guard users against insecure or unsupported configurations (e.g., MsgPack016/MsgPack008 on AOT-unsupported features) could be dropped without notice. The security impact is minimal, because these are compile-time diagnostics and not runtime protections.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the analyzer tests for MsgPack diagnostics on source-declared types, including ones that may produce Location.None, and confirm that each expected diagnostic is still reported after the wrapper.

hunches.claim: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation is applied to every diagnostic that reportDiagnostic emits, not just diagnostics from metadata symbols. Any existing diagnostic created with a null or non-compilation location (for example MsgPack004 via the FirstOrDefault()?.GetLocation() path) is now silently dropped. Ledger entries L9 and L10 record that false-positive and false-negative regressions have happened before in this area. The tests cover no same-assembly case where a diagnostic must still be reported.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the existing analyzer tests (MsgPack003, MsgPack004 and MsgPack005) for same-assembly types to confirm the diagnostics are still reported. Add a test for the MemberNeedsKey diagnostic on a source-declared generic struct.

hunches.claim: The `reportDiagnostic` wrapper `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation` is a new behavior (it drops every diagnostic whose location is not in a syntax tree of the compilation), and no test checks that diagnostics for source types in the compilation are still reported. All new tests assert only no diagnostics. A mutant that makes the filter always drop (condition negated) would pass every test in the diff.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1444 negate-condition: `if (diagnostic.Location.IsInSource && this.compilation.ContainsSyntaxTree(...))` -> `if (!(...))`; expected to survive because all new tests only expect zero diagnostics and none assert that a source-located diagnostic such as MsgPack004 is still reported

hunches.claim: The `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` change (the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull path) and the `FirstOrDefault()` change (MemberNeedsKey path) are not reliably covered. The unkeyed-member test uses a public property with no key from metadata. But the property is probably skipped earlier, because `CollectCore`/`GetObjectInfo` may return before the diagnostic path for metadata types, so the test may pass on base as well. No test reaches BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull. Reverting the `FirstOrDefault()?` fix to `[0]` may therefore survive, since the wrapper filter alone would hide the problem if the exception were not thrown.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1077 remove-guard: `item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences.FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax().GetLocation()` -> `item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0].GetSyntax().GetLocation()`; expected to survive if no test reaches this branch with a metadata symbol. Also revert the line 985 helper to `[0]` and run ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference_UnkeyedMember.

hunches.claim: The tests do not cover a negative case: a closed generic struct declared in the same assembly with an unkeyed member must still report MsgPack004. They also do not cover a closed generic class from metadata, a non-generic struct from metadata, or another generic struct from metadata (the 'ok' rows in the requirement). Nothing guards against the filter swallowing legitimate diagnostics in-source.

receipt_plan.detail: Add a test with an in-source `[MessagePackObject] struct S<T>` having an unkeyed public member, used as `S<int>` in another type, expecting MsgPack004; run it against the head build.

hunches.claim: RunWithMetadataReferenceAsync sets TestBehaviors.SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and runs the generator through a separate manual CSharpGeneratorDriver, rather than the verified test. The first run asserts only that there are no diagnostics. The second asserts only that a hint name is present, not the content. A resolver that is generated but lacks a formatter for the generic struct, or that has an incorrect one, would pass.

receipt_plan.detail: Make the collector skip the closed generic struct member in the usage type (delete the registration statement) while still emitting an empty resolver; expected to survive because only the hint name is asserted.

hunches.claim: The requirement names three unguarded `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` sites in `GetObjectInfo`, at reporter lines 735, 1009 and 1101. The diff guards only two of them: the hunks at new lines 985 and 1077 correspond to reporter lines 1009 and 1101 at the same -24 offset. Nothing touches the earlier site near reporter line 735 (about line 711 now). The new `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation` wrapper only filters a Diagnostic after it is built. It cannot stop an `IndexOutOfRangeException` thrown while computing the location argument. If that third site is reached for the metadata `Item<T>`, the generator (CS8785) and the analyzer (AD0001) still crash.

receipt_plan.detail: On head, grep src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs for `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` and confirm an unguarded index remains inside GetObjectInfo before line 985. Then run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ClosedGenericStructFromReferencedAssemblyTests (both theories, record struct and struct) on head: any CS8785 or analyzer exception proves the remaining site fires.

hunches.claim: The requirement names three unguarded `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` sites (reported lines 735, 1009, 1101). The diff changes only the two near new lines 985 and 1077. If the third site (around old line 735, in GetObjectInfo) still indexes [0], it can still throw for metadata symbols. That would happen if it is evaluated in the generator path (no ?.Invoke short-circuit) or in the analyzer path, and the wrapper does not help because the throw happens while the Diagnostic is being built, before it is reported.

receipt_plan.detail: grep head TypeCollector.cs for `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]`. Then confirm with the full two-assembly repro: lib containing `partial record struct Item<T>` as a MetadataReference, app containing Cmd with `Item<int> Member`, checking for no CS8785/AD0001.

hunches.claim: Filtering all diagnostics by tree membership also hides diagnostics for source types in the same compilation if the location came from a different compilation's syntax tree, e.g. partial or generated trees. Diagnostics previously reported are now dropped, and it is unclear whether the MemberNeedsKey fix (FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax().GetLocation()) is consistent with the wrapper for null-location members.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the TypeCollector paths that call reportDiagnostic with null or Location.None locations, and compare with base behavior. Confirm via the existing analyzer test suite that no expected diagnostic goes missing.

hunches.claim: The README adds a new top-level section and the MsgPack004 doc adds a note. No docs or tests cover the non-generic metadata path or the case where a generic type's members are in metadata but the type is a class. The 'including generic value types' claim is untested for the AOT-trimmed runtime, which is the actual failure the requirement describes.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare the README claim against the tests. They check only that generation succeeds and a resolver hint name exists. They do not check that the resolver includes a formatter for Item<int>.

hunches.claim: suppressed by unconfirmed context entry: [L8] area=analyzer, generator: Types that come from a referenced assembly are deliberately not analysed and get no formatter from the compiling assembly. In `TypeCollector.CollectCore`, after the custom-formatter, enum and generic checks, a non-generic type whose symbol is metadata-only exits with a bare `if (type.Locations[0].IsInMetadata) { return; }` (TypeCollector.cs:367-370), so no MsgPack003/004/005 diagnostic and no generated formatter appear for it. The defining assembly owns validating and formatting its own types (rationale inferred: the code has no comment). A missing diagnostic or formatter for such a type is not a defect. (source: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:367) (would-be finding: The new docs say diagnostics for members of referenced-assembly types are reported by the defining assembly. This matches the recorded deliberate behaviour that metadata types are not analysed by the consumer, so it is fine. The new ReportIfLocatedInCompilation filter drops diagnostics with no source location, which is consistent with the same entry.)

receipt_plan.detail: [L8] Types from a referenced assembly are deliberately not analysed by the compiling assembly, and a missing diagnostic for them is not a defect.
